Full evidence queries, owner names, review timestamps, and incident records are maintained in our private security registry and made available to enterprise partners under NDA. pages.aiDoctor.faqs[0].q: Is there a free AI doctor?
pages.aiDoctor.faqs[1].a: No. An AI tool can suggest possibilities, but a diagnosis needs a clinician who can examine you, order tests and weigh your full history. Treat any AI answer as information to discuss with a clinician, not as a diagnosis.
pages.aiDoctor.faqs[2].a: General chatbots can explain medical topics, but they do not know your history, can state errors confidently and may not cite sources. Check important answers with a clinician, and think twice before sharing sensitive health details with a tool that is not built to protect them.
pages.aiDoctor.faqs[2].q: Is it safe to ask ChatGPT medical questions?

pages.biomarkerA1c.faqs[0].a: An A1C of 5.7% is the lower edge of the prediabetes range. It is not diabetes, but it is a useful early warning. Many people bring it back into the usual range with changes to activity, diet and weight, and a recheck in about a year is common.
pages.biomarkerA1c.faqs[1].a: Usually not. A1C reflects the past two to three months, so a recent meal has little effect. Your clinician may still ask you to fast if other tests, such as fasting glucose or cholesterol, are drawn at the same time.
pages.biomarkerA1c.faqs[1].q: Do I need to fast for an A1C test?
pages.biomarkerA1c.faqs[2].a: Because it reflects about three months of blood sugar, A1C changes slowly. Changes in lifestyle or treatment usually start to show after six to eight weeks, with the full effect at about three months.
pages.biomarkerA1c.faqs[2].q: How fast can A1C go down?
pages.biomarkerA1c.faqs[3].a: Yes, sometimes. Iron deficiency, some hemoglobin variants and other conditions can raise A1C even when glucose is normal. That is why a single result is usually confirmed with a repeat A1C or a glucose test before diabetes is diagnosed.

pages.biomarkerA1c.lede: HbA1c, often called A1C, shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months. It is the main blood test used to screen for prediabetes and diabetes and to follow diabetes over time. This guide explains the ranges, what can make the number misleading, and what to ask next.
pages.biomarkerA1c.rangesNote: Labs report A1C as a percentage or in mmol/mol. An A1C of 7% matches an average blood sugar of about 154 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L). Always use the reference range printed on your own report.

pages.biomarkerA1c.ranges[1].label: Prediabetes range
pages.biomarkerA1c.ranges[2].label: Diabetes range
pages.biomarkerA1c.ranges[2].value: 6.5% or higher (48 mmol/mol or higher), confirmed by a repeat test
pages.biomarkerA1c.ranges[3].label: Common target with diabetes
pages.biomarkerA1c.ranges[3].value: Below 7% (53 mmol/mol); your clinician may set a different goal
pages.biomarkerA1c.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[0].body: Sugar in your blood sticks to hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Red blood cells live for about three months, so the share of hemoglobin with sugar attached reflects your average blood sugar over that time. Unlike a finger-prick or fasting glucose test, A1C does not change much from one day to the next, and you usually do not need to fast for it.
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[0].title: What does HbA1c measure?
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[1].body: An A1C below 5.7% is in the usual range. Between 5.7% and 6.4% is called prediabetes: blood sugar runs higher than ideal and the risk of type 2 diabetes is raised, but many people bring it back down. A result of 6.5% or higher suggests diabetes; clinicians normally confirm it with a second test, unless symptoms and a high glucose already make it clear.
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[1].title: Normal, prediabetes and diabetes
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[2].body: Each A1C value matches an estimated average glucose. Roughly, 6% is about 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), 7% about 154 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) and 8% about 183 mg/dL (10.2 mmol/L). Two people with the same A1C can still have very different daily highs and lows, which is why people with diabetes often also check glucose readings or use a continuous glucose monitor.
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[2].title: How A1C relates to average blood sugar
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[3].body: Anything that changes how long red blood cells live can push A1C away from your true average. Iron deficiency anemia can raise it, while recent blood loss, a transfusion, hemolysis, pregnancy and advanced kidney or liver disease can lower it. Some hemoglobin variants, such as sickle cell trait, can affect certain lab methods. If your A1C does not match your glucose readings, tell your clinician.
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[3].title: What can make A1C misleading
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[4].body: Without diabetes, adults with risk factors such as excess weight, a family history or a past high reading are commonly screened every one to three years. With prediabetes, many clinicians recheck about once a year. With diabetes, A1C is usually checked two to four times a year, more often after a change in treatment.
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[4].title: How often is A1C checked?
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[5].body: Regular physical activity, losing weight if you carry extra, fewer refined carbohydrates and sugary drinks, more fibre and vegetables, good sleep and not smoking all help lower blood sugar. In prediabetes, losing about 5% to 7% of body weight lowers the chance of developing type 2 diabetes. If medication is needed, the choice is for you and your clinician; A1C usually takes about three months to reflect a change.
pages.biomarkerA1c.sections[5].title: What can lower A1C?
pages.biomarkerA1c.seoDescription: What an HbA1c (A1C) result means: normal, prediabetes and diabetes ranges, how A1C relates to average blood sugar, what can skew it, and how to lower it.

pages.biomarkerAlt.ctaTitle: Follow your liver tests over time
pages.biomarkerAlt.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerAlt.faqs[0].a: A slightly high ALT is common and often temporary, but it is worth following up. Many cases come from fatty liver, alcohol or a medicine, and some need treatment. Your clinician will usually repeat the test and look for the cause.
pages.biomarkerAlt.faqs[0].q: Is a slightly high ALT something to worry about?
pages.biomarkerAlt.faqs[1].a: Yes. Heavy or unaccustomed exercise, especially weight training, can raise ALT and AST for several days because muscle releases them too. Avoid strenuous workouts for 24 to 48 hours before a liver test.
pages.biomarkerAlt.faqs[2].a: Regular or heavy drinking can raise liver enzymes, and alcohol often raises AST more than ALT. Even moderate drinking can add to the effect of fatty liver.
pages.biomarkerAlt.faqs[3].a: After a short-term cause such as a medicine or an infection, ALT often settles within weeks. With fatty liver, improvement usually follows weight loss and lifestyle changes over a few months.
pages.biomarkerAlt.faqs[3].q: How long does it take ALT to return to normal?
pages.biomarkerAlt.headline: ALT Blood Test Explained: What a High ALT Liver Enzyme Means
pages.biomarkerAlt.keywords: ALT blood test, high ALT, what does high ALT mean, alanine aminotransferase, ALT normal range, elevated liver enzymes, SGPT, fatty liver, AST ALT ratio
pages.biomarkerAlt.lede: ALT is the liver enzyme most often flagged on a routine blood panel. A mildly high ALT is common and frequently linked to fatty liver, alcohol or medicines; a very high ALT needs prompt attention. This guide explains what the result means and what usually comes next.
pages.biomarkerAlt.rangesNote: ALT is reported in units per litre (U/L or IU/L). Ranges vary between labs; use the one printed on your report.
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[0].label: Typical lab upper limit
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[0].value: About 35 to 56 U/L, depending on the lab
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[1].label: Healthy upper limit (ACG guidance), men
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[2].label: Healthy upper limit (ACG guidance), women
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[3].label: Mild rise
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[3].value: Up to about 5 times the upper limit
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[4].label: Very high, needs prompt care
pages.biomarkerAlt.ranges[4].value: More than about 10 to 15 times the upper limit
pages.biomarkerAlt.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[0].body: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT, also called SGPT) is an enzyme found mainly inside liver cells. When liver cells are irritated or damaged, ALT leaks into the blood, so a higher level is a sign of liver cell stress. ALT is not a measure of how well your liver works; that is judged with other tests such as albumin, bilirubin and clotting tests.
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[0].title: What is ALT?
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[1].body: The most common cause of a mildly raised ALT is fatty liver linked to excess weight, insulin resistance or diabetes (now called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, MASLD). Others include alcohol, many medicines (such as acetaminophen at high doses, some statins, antibiotics and antiseizure drugs), herbal and bodybuilding supplements, viral hepatitis B or C, and less often celiac disease, thyroid disorders or iron overload.
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[1].title: The most common causes of a high ALT
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[2].body: A very high ALT, often in the hundreds or above 1,000 U/L, can mean acute hepatitis, a medicine or supplement reaction such as an acetaminophen overdose, or reduced blood flow to the liver. Seek care the same day if a high ALT comes with yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, abdominal pain, confusion or vomiting.
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[2].title: When a high ALT is urgent
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[3].body: ALT is usually read with AST, another enzyme found in the liver and in muscle. When AST is more than about twice ALT, alcohol-related liver injury becomes more likely; when ALT is higher than AST, fatty liver and viral hepatitis are more common. A rise in both after intense exercise can come from muscle rather than the liver.
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[3].title: ALT and AST together
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[4].body: For a mild rise without symptoms, clinicians commonly repeat the test after a few weeks, review alcohol, medicines and supplements, and check for hepatitis B and C, diabetes and cholesterol. An ultrasound may look for fatty liver. If ALT stays high, further tests look for less common causes.
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[4].title: What usually happens next
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[5].body: That depends on the cause. For fatty liver, losing 7 to 10% of body weight, regular activity, and cutting back on sugary drinks and alcohol often bring ALT back toward normal within months. Never stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask your clinician whether a medicine could be the cause.
pages.biomarkerAlt.sections[5].title: What can bring ALT down?
pages.biomarkerAlt.seoDescription: What a high ALT (alanine aminotransferase, SGPT) result means: typical ranges, the most common causes such as fatty liver, and when a raised result needs a quick follow-up.

pages.biomarkerB12.ctaTitle: See your B12 next to the rest of your health
pages.biomarkerB12.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[0].a: Below about 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L) is usually considered deficient. Between 200 and 300 pg/mL (148 to 221 pmol/L) is borderline, and further tests such as methylmalonic acid help decide whether you are truly short of B12.
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[0].q: What B12 level is too low?
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[1].a: Yes. Tiredness, pins and needles, numbness and balance problems are common signs of B12 deficiency. Tell your clinician about nerve symptoms promptly, because early treatment gives the best chance of full recovery.
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[1].q: Can low B12 cause tiredness and tingling?
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[2].a: Most health bodies advise vegans to take B12 regularly, as a supplement or in fortified foods, because plant foods do not provide reliable amounts. Ask your clinician or pharmacist about the right dose.
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[2].q: Should I take a B12 supplement if I am vegan?
pages.biomarkerB12.faqs[3].a: High B12 from supplements is usually harmless because extra is passed in urine. A high level without supplements is worth discussing with your clinician, as it can sometimes point to another condition.
pages.biomarkerB12.headline: Vitamin B12 Test Explained: What Low or High B12 Means
pages.biomarkerB12.keywords: vitamin B12 test, B12 deficiency, low B12, B12 normal range, B12 levels, high B12, B12 deficiency symptoms, cobalamin, methylmalonic acid, pernicious anemia
pages.biomarkerB12.lede: Vitamin B12 helps your body make red blood cells and keeps your nerves healthy. A low level can cause tiredness, anemia and numbness or tingling, and nerve damage can become permanent if it is left untreated for a long time. This guide explains the ranges, who is more likely to run low, and what happens after a low or borderline result.
pages.biomarkerB12.rangesNote: Labs report B12 in pg/mL (the same as ng/L) or pmol/L, and cut-offs vary between labs. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.
pages.biomarkerB12.ranges[0].label: Deficient
pages.biomarkerB12.ranges[1].label: Borderline
pages.biomarkerB12.ranges[1].value: 200 to 300 pg/mL (148 to 221 pmol/L): often checked with more tests
pages.biomarkerB12.ranges[2].label: Usual range
pages.biomarkerB12.ranges[3].label: High
pages.biomarkerB12.ranges[3].value: Above about 900 pg/mL (above 664 pmol/L): usually from supplements
pages.biomarkerB12.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[0].body: Vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, is needed to make DNA and healthy red blood cells and to protect the nerves. It comes from animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and from fortified foods. To absorb it, your stomach makes a protein called intrinsic factor. Problems with the stomach or gut can cause a deficiency even with a good diet.
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[0].title: What does vitamin B12 do?
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[1].body: People who eat a vegan diet without fortified foods or supplements; adults over 50, who often make less stomach acid; people with pernicious anemia, an autoimmune condition that blocks absorption; people who have had stomach or weight-loss surgery or have Crohn's disease; and people taking metformin or acid-reducing medicines for a long time. Recreational nitrous oxide can also cause a deficiency.
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[1].title: Who is more likely to run low?
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[2].body: Symptoms can come on slowly: tiredness, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, a sore red tongue, pins and needles or numbness in the hands and feet, problems with balance, memory or mood. On a blood count, low B12 often shows as large red blood cells (a high MCV). Some people have nerve symptoms without anemia.
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[2].title: Symptoms of low B12
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[3].body: The B12 blood test is not perfect, so a borderline result is often followed by methylmalonic acid (MMA) or homocysteine, which rise when the body is short of B12. Your clinician may also check a full blood count, folate and intrinsic factor antibodies to look for pernicious anemia.
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[3].title: Borderline results and follow-up tests
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[4].body: Most high results come from supplements or injections and are not harmful. A high B12 without supplements is less common and can be linked to liver or kidney disease or some blood conditions, so your clinician may look into an unexplained high result.
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[4].title: What does a high B12 mean?
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[5].body: Depending on the cause, treatment is high-dose B12 tablets or B12 injections. Pernicious anemia and absorption problems are often treated with injections, sometimes for life. Tiredness and anemia usually improve within weeks; nerve symptoms can take longer and may not fully recover if treatment is late. Do not rely on folic acid alone: it can hide the anemia while nerve damage continues.
pages.biomarkerB12.sections[5].title: How is low B12 treated?
pages.biomarkerB12.seoDescription: What a vitamin B12 result means: deficient, borderline and usual ranges in pg/mL and pmol/L, who runs low, symptoms of deficiency, what is tested next, and treatment.

pages.biomarkerCrp.ctaTitle: Understand your CRP next to the rest of your health
pages.biomarkerCrp.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[0].a: There is no single danger number, because the cause matters more than the value. Results above 10 mg/L suggest an active infection or inflammation, and very high results (often above 100 mg/L) are common with serious bacterial infections. If a high CRP comes with fever, severe pain, shortness of breath or feeling very unwell, seek medical care promptly.
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[1].a: A very hard or long workout can raise CRP for a day or two, and long-term stress and poor sleep are linked with slightly higher levels. Avoid intense exercise the day before an hs-CRP test so the result reflects your usual level.
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[1].q: Can stress or exercise raise CRP?
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[2].a: Not on its own. An hs-CRP above 3 mg/L, measured when you are well, is linked with higher cardiovascular risk and can tip the balance when your clinician weighs cholesterol, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and family history.
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[2].q: Is a high hs-CRP a sign of heart disease?
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[3].a: Once the cause settles, CRP roughly halves every day, so it usually returns toward normal within one to two weeks after an infection clears. Persistently raised levels need a look for an ongoing cause.
pages.biomarkerCrp.faqs[3].q: How long does it take CRP to go down?
pages.biomarkerCrp.headline: CRP Blood Test Explained: What a High C-Reactive Protein Means
pages.biomarkerCrp.keywords: CRP blood test, high CRP, C-reactive protein, hs-CRP, what does high CRP mean, CRP normal range, inflammation blood test, CRP vs ESR
pages.biomarkerCrp.lede: C-reactive protein (CRP) is one of the most common blood markers of inflammation. A high result tells you that something is inflamed, but not what or where. This guide explains the two kinds of CRP test, what the numbers usually mean, and what to ask next.
pages.biomarkerCrp.rangesNote: Some labs report CRP in mg/dL: divide mg/L by 10 (10 mg/L = 1 mg/dL). Always use the reference range printed on your own report.
pages.biomarkerCrp.ranges[0].label: Standard CRP, usual
pages.biomarkerCrp.ranges[0].value: Below 10 mg/L (many labs use below 5 or below 3)
pages.biomarkerCrp.ranges[1].label: hs-CRP, lower heart risk
pages.biomarkerCrp.ranges[2].label: hs-CRP, average heart risk
pages.biomarkerCrp.ranges[3].label: hs-CRP, higher heart risk
pages.biomarkerCrp.ranges[4].label: Suggests acute infection or inflammation
pages.biomarkerCrp.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[0].body: CRP is a protein your liver releases into the blood when the body is fighting inflammation, from an infection, an injury or a long-term inflammatory condition. Levels can rise many times over within hours and fall again within days once the cause settles, which makes CRP a useful, fast-moving signal.
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[0].title: What is C-reactive protein?
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[1].body: A standard CRP test looks for clearly raised levels, for example to check for infection or to follow an inflammatory condition. A high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) test measures the same protein at much lower levels and is used to estimate cardiovascular risk alongside cholesterol and blood pressure. hs-CRP is only meaningful for heart risk when you are well: a result above 10 mg/L usually points to an acute cause and is repeated after a couple of weeks.
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[1].title: CRP and hs-CRP: two tests, two purposes
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[2].body: Bacterial and viral infections, injuries, recent surgery and flare-ups of inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease are the usual causes of a clearly high CRP. Smaller, long-term rises are linked to excess body weight, smoking, poor sleep, diabetes, gum disease and inactivity. Pregnancy and oral estrogen can also raise CRP.
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[2].title: Common reasons for a high CRP
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[3].body: CRP shows that inflammation is present, not its cause or location. Your clinician reads it with your symptoms, an examination and other tests such as a complete blood count or ESR. A single mildly raised result is common after a cold, a hard workout or a minor injury, so a repeat test is often the next step.
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[3].title: Why CRP never makes a diagnosis on its own
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[4].body: Both are inflammation markers. CRP rises within hours and falls quickly as you recover, so it tracks what is happening now. ESR (sed rate) changes more slowly and is affected by age, anemia and other proteins in the blood. Clinicians often order both together.
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[4].title: CRP vs ESR
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[5].body: The main step is treating the underlying cause. For long-term, low-grade inflammation, regular physical activity, losing weight if you carry extra, not smoking, good sleep and a Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish and olive oil are linked with lower CRP. Some medicines, including statins, also lower it; whether you need one is a decision for you and your clinician.
pages.biomarkerCrp.sections[5].title: What can lower CRP?
pages.biomarkerCrp.seoDescription: What a CRP or hs-CRP result means: typical ranges, common reasons for a high CRP, how it differs from ESR, and what lowers it. A plain-language guide.

pages.biomarkerEgfr.ctaTitle: Understand your eGFR next to the rest of your health
pages.biomarkerEgfr.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.faqs[0].a: An eGFR of 60 is at the border of the mildly decreased range. On its own it is not a diagnosis of kidney disease, especially in older adults. Your clinician will usually repeat it, check urine albumin and look at your blood pressure and blood sugar.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.faqs[1].a: Yes, it can. A low reading caused by dehydration, illness or a medicine often returns toward normal once the cause is fixed. In long-term kidney disease, the aim is usually to slow or stop the decline, which good blood pressure and blood sugar control can do.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.faqs[2].a: If you were dehydrated, drinking enough fluid can bring a temporarily low eGFR back up. Drinking far more than you need does not improve kidney function, and people with advanced kidney disease may be advised to limit fluid.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.faqs[2].q: Does drinking more water raise eGFR?
pages.biomarkerEgfr.faqs[3].a: Creatinine is a waste product from muscles that the kidneys clear from the blood. eGFR is calculated from creatinine, age and sex to estimate filtering. A higher creatinine usually means a lower eGFR.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.faqs[3].q: What is the difference between creatinine and eGFR?
pages.biomarkerEgfr.headline: eGFR Explained: What Your Kidney Function Number Means
pages.biomarkerEgfr.keywords: eGFR test, eGFR blood test, low eGFR, eGFR normal range, what does eGFR mean, kidney function test, eGFR 60, creatinine and eGFR, CKD stages eGFR
pages.biomarkerEgfr.lede: eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate, is a number calculated from a blood test that shows how well your kidneys filter waste. It usually comes with your creatinine result. A lower eGFR means the kidneys are filtering less, but one low reading does not mean kidney disease. This guide explains the stages and what is checked next.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.rangesNote: Chronic kidney disease is diagnosed only when eGFR stays below 60, or there are other signs of kidney damage such as albumin in the urine, for at least three months. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[0].label: Normal or high
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[1].label: Mildly decreased
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[1].value: 60 to 89, often normal with age unless there are other signs of kidney damage
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[2].label: Mild to moderate decrease (stage 3a)
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[3].label: Moderate to severe decrease (stage 3b)
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[4].label: Severe decrease (stage 4)
pages.biomarkerEgfr.ranges[5].label: Kidney failure (stage 5)
pages.biomarkerEgfr.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[0].body: Your kidneys filter waste and extra fluid from the blood through millions of tiny filters called glomeruli. eGFR estimates how much blood they filter each minute. It is calculated from your blood creatinine level together with your age and sex, and sometimes from another marker called cystatin C. Most labs now use equations that do not include race.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[0].title: What is eGFR?
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[1].body: eGFR can drop for a short time with dehydration, a recent large meat meal, intense exercise, illness and some medicines, including anti-inflammatory painkillers. Very muscular people can have a falsely low eGFR, and people with low muscle mass a falsely high one. That is why a low result is usually repeated, and chronic kidney disease is only diagnosed when it stays low for three months or more.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[1].title: Why one low result is not a diagnosis
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[2].body: Clinicians look at kidney health with two tests: eGFR, which shows filtering, and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), which shows whether protein is leaking into the urine. An ACR above 30 mg/g (3 mg/mmol) is a sign of kidney damage even when eGFR is normal. Together they set the stage of kidney disease and guide how often to recheck.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[2].title: eGFR and urine albumin together
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[3].body: The most common long-term causes are diabetes and high blood pressure. Others include kidney inflammation, polycystic kidney disease, repeated kidney infections, blockages and long-term use of some medicines. eGFR also tends to fall slowly with age, so a reading between 60 and 89 in an older adult may be normal if there are no other signs of kidney damage.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[3].title: Common reasons for a lower eGFR
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[4].body: A sudden drop in eGFR, a result below 30, or a low eGFR with symptoms such as much less urine, swelling of the legs or face, breathlessness, confusion or nausea needs prompt medical care. A steady fall over several tests, even within the normal range, is also worth discussing with your clinician.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[4].title: When a low or falling eGFR needs quick follow-up
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[5].body: Keeping blood pressure and blood sugar in your target range is the most important step. Not smoking, staying active, keeping a healthy weight, limiting salt and avoiding regular use of anti-inflammatory painkillers also help. Some blood pressure and diabetes medicines also protect the kidneys; whether you need one is a decision for you and your clinician.
pages.biomarkerEgfr.sections[5].title: How to protect your kidneys
pages.biomarkerEgfr.seoDescription: What an eGFR result means: the kidney function stages, why a single low eGFR is not a diagnosis, how creatinine and urine albumin fit in, and how to protect your kidneys.
pages.biomarkerEsr.ctaBody: Add your results to VHT to see ESR and CRP side by side with your symptoms and history, and ECHNA, your AI health assistant, explains what changed in plain language.
pages.biomarkerEsr.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerEsr.faqs[0].a: It depends on age and sex, but results well above the age-adjusted limit, and especially above 100 mm/hr, need a search for the cause. A mildly high ESR without symptoms is common and is often simply rechecked.
pages.biomarkerEsr.faqs[1].a: Yes. ESR is higher with age, in women, during pregnancy and with anemia. A mild rise may have no significant cause, which is why it is read together with your symptoms and other tests.
pages.biomarkerEsr.faqs[1].q: Can a high ESR be normal?
pages.biomarkerEsr.faqs[2].a: Neither is better overall. CRP responds faster and is less affected by other factors, so it is often preferred for infection. ESR remains useful for some inflammatory conditions. Many clinicians order both.
pages.biomarkerEsr.faqs[3].a: ESR is not a cancer test. Some cancers raise it, but most high results have other causes, and a normal ESR does not rule cancer out.
pages.biomarkerEsr.headline: ESR Blood Test Explained: What a High Sed Rate Means
pages.biomarkerEsr.keywords: ESR blood test, high ESR, what does high ESR mean, sed rate, sedimentation rate, ESR normal range by age, ESR vs CRP, inflammation blood test
pages.biomarkerEsr.lede: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, or sed rate) is one of the oldest blood tests for inflammation. It is simple and inexpensive but not specific: a high ESR says inflammation may be present, not where or why. This guide explains how to read it and when it matters.
pages.biomarkerEsr.rangesNote: ESR is reported in millimetres per hour (mm/hr). Ranges vary between labs; use the one printed on your report.
pages.biomarkerEsr.ranges[0].label: Men under 50
pages.biomarkerEsr.ranges[1].label: Men 50 and over
pages.biomarkerEsr.ranges[2].label: Women under 50
pages.biomarkerEsr.ranges[3].label: Women 50 and over
pages.biomarkerEsr.ranges[4].label: Rule of thumb for the upper limit
pages.biomarkerEsr.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[0].body: ESR measures how far red blood cells settle to the bottom of a tall, thin tube in one hour. During inflammation, proteins such as fibrinogen make red cells clump together, so they fall faster and the ESR is higher.
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[0].title: What does ESR measure?
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[1].body: ESR naturally rises with age and is usually higher in women. A result that would be high for a 25-year-old can be normal at 75. That is why labs and clinicians use age- and sex-adjusted limits.
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[1].title: Why normal ESR rises with age
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[2].body: Infections, autoimmune and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, anemia, kidney disease, pregnancy and older age. A very high ESR, often above 100 mm/hr, can come with serious infection, inflammation of blood vessels, or blood cancers such as multiple myeloma, and always needs follow-up.
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[2].title: Common reasons for a high ESR
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[3].body: In people over 50, a new headache, tenderness of the scalp or temples, jaw pain when chewing, or any change in vision together with a high ESR can be a sign of giant cell arteritis. This needs same-day medical care because it can threaten sight.
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[3].title: When a high ESR is urgent
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[4].body: Both measure inflammation. CRP rises and falls within days, so it tracks what is happening now. ESR changes over weeks and is also affected by anemia and blood proteins. ESR is still useful for following conditions such as polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis.
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[4].title: ESR vs CRP
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[5].body: A low ESR is rarely a concern. It can be seen with a high red cell count (polycythemia), sickle cell disease or a very high white cell count, and is usually not followed up on its own.
pages.biomarkerEsr.sections[5].title: What about a low ESR?

pages.biomarkerFerritin.faqs[0].a: Below about 30 ng/mL usually means iron stores are low, and below 15 ng/mL strongly suggests iron deficiency, even if your lab’s range starts lower. Your clinician will look at your symptoms, blood count and the likely cause before deciding on treatment.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.faqs[0].q: What ferritin level is too low?
pages.biomarkerFerritin.faqs[1].a: It can. Low iron stores, with or without anemia, are linked with tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance in some people. Tiredness has many causes, though, so it is worth discussing the whole picture with your clinician.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.faqs[2].a: It depends on the cause. Most mildly high results reflect inflammation, fatty liver or alcohol and are not dangerous in themselves, but the cause is worth finding. Very high ferritin, or a high ferritin with a high transferrin saturation, needs prompt follow-up.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.faqs[3].a: With iron treatment, hemoglobin often improves within a few weeks, but refilling iron stores usually takes about three months or more. Your clinician will usually recheck ferritin after a course of treatment.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.faqs[3].q: How long does it take to raise ferritin?

pages.biomarkerFerritin.lede: Ferritin is the protein that stores iron in your body, and the amount in your blood is a good guide to how much iron you have in reserve. A low ferritin is the clearest early sign of iron deficiency. A high ferritin is less simple: it can mean too much iron, but more often it reflects inflammation or a liver problem. This guide explains both.

pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[0].body: Your body stores most of its spare iron inside ferritin, mainly in the liver, spleen and bone marrow. A small amount of ferritin circulates in the blood, and its level rises and falls with your iron stores. That makes ferritin the most useful single blood test for spotting iron deficiency early, before anemia develops.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[1].body: A low ferritin almost always means your iron stores are running low. Common causes are heavy periods, pregnancy, blood donation, a diet low in iron, and blood loss from the gut, for example from ulcers, polyps or regular use of anti-inflammatory painkillers. Problems absorbing iron, as in coeliac disease, can also lower it. In adults, especially men and women after menopause, unexplained low iron usually needs a check for a hidden cause.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[1].titl: What a low ferritin usually means
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[2].body: Ferritin falls before hemoglobin does, so you can have low iron stores with a normal blood count. Some people in this stage feel tired, short of breath on exertion, notice hair shedding or restless legs, though these symptoms have many causes. Your clinician may look at your hemoglobin, MCV, MCH and transferrin saturation with ferritin to see the full picture.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[3].body: Ferritin also rises as part of the body’s response to inflammation, so a high result most often reflects an infection, an inflammatory condition, fatty liver, regular alcohol use, obesity or metabolic syndrome rather than extra iron. Less often it points to iron overload, such as hereditary hemochromatosis, or to repeated blood transfusions. Transferrin saturation helps tell these apart: when it is also high, iron overload is more likely.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[3].titl: What a high ferritin usually means
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[4].body: Because inflammation pushes ferritin up, a normal or high result can hide low iron in someone who is unwell. Clinicians often check CRP, transferrin saturation, serum iron and a complete blood count alongside ferritin. A single mildly abnormal result is common and is often repeated.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[4].titl: Why ferritin is read with other tests
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[5].body: Low iron stores are usually treated with iron-rich foods and often an iron supplement, together with finding the cause. Taking iron with vitamin C and apart from tea, coffee and calcium can improve absorption. Do not start high-dose iron without advice, because too much iron is harmful. For high ferritin, the plan depends on the cause; treating inflammation, fatty liver or alcohol use often brings it down, and iron overload is managed by a specialist.
pages.biomarkerFerritin.sections[5].titl: How low or high ferritin is managed
pages.biomarkerFerritin.seoDescription: What a ferritin result means: typical ranges, why low ferritin is the clearest sign of low iron stores, common reasons ferritin runs high, and what is checked next.

pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[0].a: A fasting glucose of 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) is the lower edge of the prediabetes range in many countries. It is not diabetes, but it is a useful early warning. A repeat test or an HbA1c helps confirm it, and many people bring it down with changes to activity, diet and weight.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[0].q: Is a fasting blood sugar of 100 bad?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[1].a: Usually at least 8 hours, with only water. Most people have the test first thing in the morning. Take your usual medicines unless your clinician tells you otherwise.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[1].q: How long do I need to fast before a glucose test?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[2].a: Hormones released in the early morning, such as cortisol and growth hormone, raise blood sugar before you wake up. This is called the dawn phenomenon. It is common and usually mild, but it can push a fasting result up, especially with diabetes.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[2].q: Why is my blood sugar higher in the morning?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[3].a: They answer different questions. Fasting glucose is a snapshot of one morning; HbA1c is an average over about three months. Clinicians often use both, and one can confirm the other.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.faqs[3].q: Which is better, fasting glucose or HbA1c?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.headline: Fasting Blood Glucose Explained: What Your Blood Sugar Number Means

pages.biomarkerGlucose.lede: A fasting blood glucose test measures the sugar in your blood after at least 8 hours without food. It is one of the main tests used to screen for prediabetes and diabetes. Unlike HbA1c, which reflects the past few months, it is a snapshot of one morning. This guide explains the ranges, what can throw the number off, and what is tested next.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.rangesNote: Some countries start the prediabetes range at 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L). To convert, divide mg/dL by 18 to get mmol/L. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.

pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[0].body: Glucose is the main sugar your body uses for energy. After you eat, glucose rises and insulin moves it into your cells. After a night without food, your blood sugar should settle back into a steady range. A fasting result above that range suggests your body is not handling glucose as well as it should, often because of insulin resistance.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[0].title: What does a fasting glucose test measure?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[1].body: A fasting glucose of 70 to 99 mg/dL (3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L) is normal. From 100 to 125 mg/dL (5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L) is called impaired fasting glucose, a form of prediabetes that raises the risk of type 2 diabetes. A result of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher on two separate days, or with an HbA1c of 6.5% or more, points to diabetes.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[1].title: Normal, prediabetes and diabetes
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[2].body: Eating or drinking anything but water before the test, a recent illness or infection, stress, poor sleep, and medicines such as steroids can raise glucose. Many people also have a natural early-morning rise in blood sugar. Heavy exercise the day before can lower it. If a result surprises you, ask whether to repeat it.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[2].title: What can throw the result off?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[3].body: A high fasting result is usually repeated, often with an HbA1c, which shows your average over two to three months. Your clinician may also suggest an oral glucose tolerance test, in which glucose is measured before and two hours after a sweet drink. A random glucose of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more with symptoms such as thirst and frequent urination also suggests diabetes.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[3].title: What is tested next?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[4].body: A level below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) is low, and below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) is significantly low. Symptoms include shaking, sweating, a fast heartbeat, hunger and confusion. It mainly happens in people taking insulin or some diabetes tablets. Low blood sugar without diabetes is uncommon and worth discussing with a clinician. If someone with low blood sugar is confused, very drowsy or cannot swallow safely, call your local emergency number.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[4].title: Low blood sugar
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[5].body: Regular activity, including a short walk after meals, losing weight if you carry extra, fewer sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, more fibre, enough sleep and not smoking all help your body use insulin better. In prediabetes, losing about 5% to 7% of body weight lowers the chance of developing type 2 diabetes. If medication is needed, that choice is for you and your clinician.
pages.biomarkerGlucose.sections[5].title: What can lower fasting glucose?
pages.biomarkerGlucose.seoDescription: What a fasting blood sugar result means: normal, prediabetes and diabetes ranges in mg/dL and mmol/L, low blood sugar, what can skew the test, and what to ask next.

pages.biomarkerHdl.faqs[0].a: For most adults, 40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L) or more for men and 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L) or more for women is in the usual range, and around 60 mg/dL (1.5 mmol/L) is often considered good. Your clinician reads it alongside LDL, triglycerides and your other risk factors.
pages.biomarkerHdl.faqs[0].q: What is a good HDL level?
pages.biomarkerHdl.faqs[1].a: Low HDL is a risk factor for heart disease, not a disease in itself. It matters most when other risks are present, such as high LDL, high blood pressure, diabetes or smoking. Your clinician uses it as part of your overall heart risk.
pages.biomarkerHdl.faqs[2].a: Very high HDL, roughly above 80 to 100 mg/dL (2.0 to 2.5 mmol/L), does not seem to give extra protection and can sometimes come with other conditions. It is not usually a cause for concern on its own, but it is worth mentioning to your clinician.
pages.biomarkerHdl.faqs[3].a: Some medicines raise HDL, but trials have not shown that raising HDL with drugs prevents heart attacks. Treatment usually focuses on lowering LDL and your overall risk instead.
pages.biomarkerHdl.faqs[3].q: Is there a medicine to raise HDL?

pages.biomarkerHdl.lede: HDL is often called “good” cholesterol because it carries cholesterol away from your arteries to the liver. A low HDL is linked to a higher risk of heart disease, but HDL is only one part of the picture. This guide explains the ranges, what affects HDL, and how it fits with LDL and triglycerides.
pages.biomarkerHdl.rangesNote: HDL is usually reported as part of a lipid panel, in mg/dL or mmol/L. Cut-offs differ a little between countries and labs. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.

pages.biomarkerHdl.ranges[3].label: Higher

pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[0].body: Cholesterol travels in the blood inside particles called lipoproteins. HDL (high-density lipoprotein) picks up extra cholesterol from the body, including from artery walls, and brings it back to the liver to be cleared. That is why higher HDL has long been linked to a lower risk of heart attack and stroke, and low HDL to a higher risk.
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[0].title: What does HDL do?
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[1].body: Common reasons include the genes you inherit, little physical activity, excess weight around the waist, insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides and smoking. Some medicines, such as anabolic steroids, some progestins and certain blood pressure drugs, can lower HDL too. Low HDL often travels with high triglycerides as part of metabolic syndrome.
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[1].title: What causes low HDL?
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[2].body: Not always. Up to about 60 mg/dL (1.5 mmol/L), higher HDL goes with lower risk. Above about 80 to 100 mg/dL (2.0 to 2.5 mmol/L), studies show the benefit levels off, and very high HDL is sometimes linked to higher risk, often because of genes or other conditions. Medicines that raise HDL have not been shown to prevent heart attacks, so HDL on its own is not a treatment target.
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[2].title: Is higher HDL always better?
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[3].body: Clinicians look at HDL together with LDL, triglycerides and total cholesterol. Non-HDL cholesterol (total cholesterol minus HDL) counts all the cholesterol that can build up in arteries and is often a better guide than HDL alone. The ratio of total cholesterol to HDL is also used; a lower ratio is better. Heart risk calculators combine these with age, blood pressure, smoking and diabetes.
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[3].title: How HDL fits with the rest of your lipid panel
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[4].body: Less than triglycerides, but it does vary. A recent illness, a big change in weight or diet, and some medicines can shift it. You usually do not need to fast for HDL, although your clinician may ask you to fast if triglycerides are measured at the same time. One result is best read together with earlier ones.
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[4].title: Does HDL change from day to day?
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[5].body: Regular aerobic exercise, losing weight if you carry extra, stopping smoking, and swapping refined carbohydrates and trans fats for whole foods and unsaturated fats can raise HDL a little. These changes also lower LDL and triglycerides, which matters more for your heart. Alcohol can raise HDL, but drinking is not recommended as a way to do so.
pages.biomarkerHdl.sections[5].title: What can raise HDL?

pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[0].a: For an average-risk adult, an LDL above 190 mg/dL (4.9 mmol/L) is considered very high and is usually treated aggressively regardless of other factors. For people with existing heart disease, diabetes, or a strong family history, levels above 70–100 mg/dL may warrant treatment depending on overall risk.
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[0].q: What is considered a dangerous LDL cholesterol level?
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[1].a: Many people can lower LDL by 10–30% through diet (more soluble fiber and unsaturated fat, less saturated and trans fat), regular aerobic exercise, weight loss, and quitting smoking. Whether that is enough depends on your starting LDL and overall cardiovascular risk; some genetic conditions require medication regardless of lifestyle.
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[1].q: Can I lower LDL cholesterol without medication?
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[2].a: Healthy adults typically check a lipid panel every 4–6 years starting in their 20s, more often after age 40 or when risk factors are present. People on cholesterol medication or actively changing their lifestyle usually re-test every 3–12 months to track progress.
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[2].q: How often should I test my LDL cholesterol?
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[3].a: No. HDL ("good") cholesterol, triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B (ApoB) each add important information. ApoB in particular reflects the total number of atherogenic particles and is increasingly favored over LDL alone for risk assessment.
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[3].q: Is LDL the only cholesterol number that matters?
pages.biomarkerLdl.faqs[4].a: VHT.ai's digital twin imports lab results from your providers and Apple Health, then plots LDL alongside HDL, triglycerides, blood pressure, weight, activity, sleep, and medications. ECHNA, our clinical AI, flags meaningful trend changes — not noisy single-point spikes — and explains what is driving them in plain language.

pages.biomarkerLdl.keywords: LDL cholesterol, LDL levels, bad cholesterol, lower LDL, cholesterol ranges, lipid panel, ApoB, statins, digital health twin
pages.biomarkerLdl.lede: LDL cholesterol is one of the most-tested and most-misunderstood numbers on a routine lab panel. This guide explains what it really measures, what a healthy range looks like for you, and how VHT.ai's digital health twin makes the long-term trend actionable.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[0].body: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol carries cholesterol from the liver to cells throughout the body. It is often called "bad" cholesterol because, when levels stay elevated over time, LDL particles deposit cholesterol inside artery walls, forming plaque that narrows blood vessels and raises the long-term risk of heart attack and stroke. LDL itself is not poison — your body needs cholesterol to build cell membranes, hormones, and vitamin D — but the balance matters.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[0].title: What is LDL cholesterol?
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[1].body: LDL is reported in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) in the United States and millimoles per liter (mmol/L) in most other countries. A standard lipid panel measures total cholesterol, HDL, triglycerides, and either calculates or directly measures LDL. Most labs still use the Friedewald equation; a direct LDL test or an apolipoprotein B (ApoB) test is more accurate when triglycerides are high or LDL is very low.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[1].title: How LDL cholesterol is measured
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[2].body: For most healthy adults, an LDL under 100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) is considered optimal. 100–129 is near optimal, 130–159 borderline high, 160–189 high, and 190+ very high. People who already have cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or genetic conditions like familial hypercholesterolemia generally target LDL under 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L), and sometimes under 55 mg/dL with newer guidelines. Your specific target depends on your overall cardiovascular risk — your clinician should set it with you, not a generic chart.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[2].title: What is a healthy LDL range?
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[3].body: LDL fluctuates with diet, alcohol, weight changes, recent illness, and even seasonal patterns. A single high or low result can be misleading. What matters far more is the trend over months and years, and how LDL moves alongside HDL, triglycerides, blood pressure, weight, activity, and inflammatory markers. This is exactly the kind of multi-signal pattern a digital health twin is built to surface.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[3].title: Why a single LDL reading is not enough
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[4].body: Reducing saturated fat (red meat, butter, full-fat dairy, tropical oils) and eliminating trans fats has the largest dietary impact. Adding soluble fiber (oats, beans, lentils, apples, psyllium), plant sterols, fatty fish, nuts, and olive oil consistently lowers LDL in randomized trials. Regular aerobic exercise, losing 5–10% of body weight if overweight, and stopping smoking all contribute. Lifestyle alone can move LDL by 10–30% for many people — meaningful but not always sufficient.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[4].title: Lifestyle changes that lower LDL
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[5].body: Statins remain first-line therapy and reduce cardiovascular events even in people with only moderately elevated LDL when overall risk is high. Ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, PCSK9 inhibitors, and inclisiran are options when statins alone are insufficient, not tolerated, or contraindicated. The decision is never about LDL alone — it weighs your 10-year cardiovascular risk, family history, other conditions, and personal preference. A digital twin makes this conversation faster by putting the full picture in one place.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[5].title: When medications come into play
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[6].body: Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) affects roughly 1 in 250 people and causes lifelong, very high LDL from birth. It dramatically raises early heart-attack risk but is highly treatable when caught. Red flags include LDL above 190 mg/dL in an adult or above 160 in a child, a parent or sibling with early heart disease (men under 55, women under 65), or tendon xanthomas. If any of these apply, ask your clinician about genetic screening.
pages.biomarkerLdl.sections[6].title: Family history and genetic LDL elevation

pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[0].a: No. Iron deficiency is the most common cause, but thalassemia trait can produce a similar pattern. Ferritin and iron studies help tell them apart, which matters because iron tablets do not help thalassemia trait.
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[0].q: Is a low MCH always iron deficiency?
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[1].a: Yes. Low vitamin B12 or folate leads to larger red cells that hold more hemoglobin each, so MCH and MCV rise together.
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[1].q: Can vitamin B12 deficiency cause a high MCH?
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[2].a: MCH is the amount of hemoglobin per cell; MCHC is how concentrated it is inside the cell. A large cell can have a high MCH but a normal MCHC.
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[2].q: What is the difference between MCH and MCHC?
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[3].a: If the cause is low iron, B12 or folate, foods rich in them help, and supplements are often needed. Ask your clinician to confirm the cause first, because too much iron can be harmful.
pages.biomarkerMch.faqs[3].q: Can I raise my MCH with diet?

pages.biomarkerMch.lede: MCH is one of the red cell indices on a complete blood count (CBC). It tells you how much hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein, the average red blood cell holds. A low or high MCH is a clue that helps your clinician find the type and cause of anemia.
pages.biomarkerMch.rangesNote: MCH is reported in picograms (pg). Ranges vary slightly between labs; use the one printed on your report.
pages.biomarkerMch.ranges[0].label: MCH, usual
pages.biomarkerMch.ranges[1].label: MCHC, usual
pages.biomarkerMch.ranges[2].label: MCV, usual

pages.biomarkerMch.sections[0].body: MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) is the average amount of hemoglobin in one red blood cell. It is calculated from your hemoglobin and red cell count, not measured separately, so it moves closely with MCV, the average size of your red cells: bigger cells usually hold more hemoglobin.
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[0].title: What is MCH?
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[1].body: MCV is the average cell size. MCH is the average amount of hemoglobin per cell. MCHC is the concentration of hemoglobin inside the cells, so it adjusts for size. Clinicians read all three, plus hemoglobin and RDW, to classify an anemia as small-cell, normal-cell or large-cell.
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[1].title: MCH, MCHC and MCV: how they differ
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[2].body: A low MCH means red cells carry less hemoglobin than usual and are often smaller and paler. The most common cause is iron deficiency, from low intake, heavy periods, pregnancy or slow blood loss. Thalassemia trait, an inherited and often harmless condition, is another common cause; less often it comes from long-term inflammation or kidney disease.
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[2].title: Common reasons for a low MCH
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[3].body: A high MCH usually comes with large red cells (high MCV). Common causes are low vitamin B12 or folate, regular heavy alcohol use, liver disease, an underactive thyroid and some medicines, such as methotrexate, hydroxyurea and certain HIV treatments.
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[3].title: Common reasons for a high MCH
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[4].body: An MCH just outside the range with a normal hemoglobin is common and often not significant. It matters more when hemoglobin is low (anemia) or when you have symptoms such as tiredness, shortness of breath, pale skin, a fast heartbeat, or numbness and tingling, which can come with B12 deficiency.
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[4].title: When MCH matters most
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[5].body: Depending on the pattern, clinicians commonly check ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12, folate and thyroid function, and sometimes hemoglobin tests for thalassemia. Treatment targets the cause; MCH tends to normalise over a few months as new red cells are made.
pages.biomarkerMch.sections[5].title: What usually happens next
pages.biomarkerMch.seoDescription: What MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) on your complete blood count means: typical ranges, common causes of low or high MCH, and how it relates to MCV and MCHC.
pages.biomarkerRdw.ctaBody: Add your results to VHT to keep every complete blood count in one timeline, and ECHNA, your AI health assistant, explains how RDW, MCV and hemoglobin moved together.
pages.biomarkerRdw.ctaTitle: See your blood count as a trend
pages.biomarkerRdw.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[0].a: A high RDW on its own is a clue, not a diagnosis. If the rest of your blood count is normal, your clinician may simply repeat it. If hemoglobin or MCV is also abnormal, the next step is usually tests for iron, vitamin B12 and folate.
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[0].q: Should I be worried about a high RDW?
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[1].a: Yes. Iron deficiency is one of the most common causes. RDW often rises early, sometimes before hemoglobin falls, because new red cells made with too little iron are smaller than older ones.
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[1].q: Can low iron cause a high RDW?
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[2].a: Dehydration mainly affects concentration-based results such as hemoglobin and hematocrit. It does not usually change RDW in a meaningful way.
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[3].a: Red blood cells live about 120 days, so after the cause is treated RDW typically improves over two to four months as new, uniform cells replace older ones.
pages.biomarkerRdw.faqs[3].q: How long does it take RDW to return to normal?
pages.biomarkerRdw.headline: RDW Blood Test Explained: What a High Red Cell Distribution Width Means
pages.biomarkerRdw.keywords: RDW blood test, high RDW, what does high RDW mean, red cell distribution width, RDW-CV, RDW-SD, RDW normal range, complete blood count, anisocytosis
pages.biomarkerRdw.lede: RDW is one of the less familiar numbers on a complete blood count (CBC). It measures how much your red blood cells vary in size. On its own it says little, but read with MCV and hemoglobin it helps your clinician narrow down the cause of anemia or a nutrient deficiency.
pages.biomarkerRdw.rangesNote: Labs report RDW as a percentage (RDW-CV), in femtolitres (RDW-SD), or both. Use the range printed on your report.
pages.biomarkerRdw.ranges[0].label: RDW-CV, usual
pages.biomarkerRdw.ranges[1].label: RDW-SD, usual
pages.biomarkerRdw.ranges[2].label: High RDW
pages.biomarkerRdw.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[0].body: Red blood cells are normally similar in size. RDW (red cell distribution width) shows how much they vary. A high RDW means your blood contains a wider mix of small and large cells (called anisocytosis), often because new cells are being made under different conditions than older ones, for example as iron runs low.
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[0].title: What does RDW measure?
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[1].body: MCV is the average size of your red cells. Together the two are more useful: a high RDW with a low MCV often points to iron deficiency; a high RDW with a high MCV can point to low vitamin B12 or folate, or liver disease; a normal RDW with a low MCV is typical of thalassemia trait. A high RDW with a normal MCV can mean an early deficiency or two deficiencies at once.
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[1].title: Reading RDW with MCV
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[2].body: Iron deficiency (from low intake, heavy periods, pregnancy or blood loss), vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, recent bleeding, a recent blood transfusion, hemolysis (red cells breaking down early), liver disease, heavy alcohol use and some cancer treatments. A slightly high RDW with an otherwise normal blood count is common and often not significant.
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[2].title: Common reasons for a high RDW
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[3].body: A low RDW means your red cells are very uniform in size. It is rarely a sign of a problem on its own and usually does not need follow-up.
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[3].title: What about a low RDW?
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[4].body: In large studies, a persistently high RDW is linked with higher rates of heart disease and other chronic conditions. This is an association, not a diagnosis, and RDW is not used on its own to judge your risk. It is one more reason to look at the trend in your blood counts over time.
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[4].title: RDW and long-term health
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[5].body: If RDW is high together with an abnormal hemoglobin or MCV, clinicians often check ferritin (iron stores), vitamin B12, folate and sometimes a reticulocyte count or blood smear. Treatment is aimed at the cause, for example iron or vitamin replacement, and RDW usually returns toward normal over a few months as new red cells replace old ones.
pages.biomarkerRdw.sections[5].title: What usually happens next
pages.biomarkerRdw.seoDescription: What a high RDW on your complete blood count means: typical ranges, how RDW reads with MCV to point toward iron, B12 or folate deficiency, and what to ask next.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.ctaBody: Add your results to VHT and see triglycerides alongside your other labs, meals, activity and history, and ECHNA, your AI health assistant, explains what changed in plain language.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.ctaTitle: See your triglycerides next to your meals and activity
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.disclaimerB: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[0].a: A fasting level of 200 mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L) is in the high range. It is not an emergency, but it is a sign to look at diet, alcohol, activity and weight, and to check blood sugar and the rest of the lipid panel. Many people bring it down with lifestyle changes.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[0].q: Is a triglyceride level of 200 bad?
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[1].a: Faster than most lab values. Cutting alcohol and sugar can lower triglycerides noticeably within a few weeks. A repeat test after about 6 to 12 weeks of changes shows the effect.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[1].q: How fast can triglycerides go down?
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[2].a: Yes. Genes, alcohol, a diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrates, an underactive thyroid, diabetes and some medicines can raise triglycerides at any weight.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[2].q: Can thin people have high triglycerides?
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[3].a: Prescription-strength omega-3 can lower high triglycerides, but over-the-counter fish oil varies in dose and quality. Talk to your clinician before starting it, especially if you take blood thinners.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.faqs[3].q: Should I take fish oil for high triglycerides?
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.headline: Triglycerides Test Explained: What High Triglycerides Mean
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.keywords: triglycerides, high triglycerides, triglycerides normal range, what are triglycerides, how to lower triglycerides, triglycerides blood test, fasting triglycerides, triglycerides 200
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.lede: Triglycerides are the most common type of fat in your blood. Your body stores extra calories as triglycerides and releases them for energy between meals. High levels are linked to heart disease, and very high levels can inflame the pancreas. This guide explains the ranges, what pushes triglycerides up, and what brings them down.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.rangesNote: Labs report triglycerides in mg/dL or mmol/L. A non-fasting result below 175 mg/dL (2.0 mmol/L) is usually fine. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.rangesTitle: Typical fasting ranges at a glance
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.ranges[3].v: 500 mg/dL or more (5.6 mmol/L or more): raises the risk of pancreatitis
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.secondaryCt: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.sections[0]: When you eat more calories than you need, especially from sugar, refined carbohydrates and alcohol, your liver turns the extra into triglycerides. They travel in the blood and are stored in fat cells until your body needs energy. Levels rise after a meal and fall again over several hours, which is why the timing of the test matters.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.sections[1]: Many labs now accept a non-fasting lipid panel for routine checks. If your non-fasting triglycerides come back high, usually above 400 mg/dL (4.5 mmol/L), your clinician will often repeat the test after an 8 to 12 hour fast. Avoiding alcohol and a very fatty meal the day before also gives a more accurate result.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.sections[2]: Common causes are excess weight, little physical activity, a diet high in sugar, refined carbohydrates and alcohol, insulin resistance and poorly controlled diabetes. An underactive thyroid, kidney disease and some medicines, including oral estrogen, steroids, some diuretics, retinoids and certain antipsychotics, can raise them too. Some people inherit a tendency to high triglycerides.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.sections[3]: Above about 500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), and especially above 1,000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L), triglycerides can cause pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas. Talk to your clinician soon about a result in this range. Severe pain in the upper belly that spreads to the back, often with nausea or vomiting, needs urgent care the same day.
Why very high levels need prompt care
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.sections[4]: High triglycerides often come with low HDL, small dense LDL particles and insulin resistance, a pattern linked to heart disease. Clinicians read triglycerides together with LDL, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol, blood pressure and blood sugar to judge your overall heart risk.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.sections[5]: Triglycerides respond quickly to lifestyle changes. Cutting back on sugary drinks, sweets, refined carbohydrates and alcohol, losing weight if you carry extra, regular exercise and eating fish rich in omega-3 fats can lower them noticeably within weeks. If they stay high, your clinician may suggest medicine, such as a statin, a fibrate or prescription omega-3, depending on your levels and overall risk.
pages.biomarkerTriglycerides.seoDescript: What a triglyceride result means: normal, borderline, high and very high ranges, common causes, when to fast, why very high levels need prompt care, and how to lower them.

pages.biomarkerTsh.ctaTitle: Understand your TSH next to the rest of your health
pages.biomarkerTsh.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerTsh.faqs[0].a: Most labs flag results above about 4.0 to 4.5 mIU/L. Between that and 10 mIU/L, clinicians often repeat the test and check free T4 before deciding on treatment. Above 10 mIU/L, treatment is more often recommended, but the decision depends on symptoms, age, pregnancy plans and other results.
pages.biomarkerTsh.faqs[0].q: What TSH level is too high?
pages.biomarkerTsh.faqs[1].a: Short-term stress has little direct effect, but serious illness, poor sleep and some medicines can shift TSH for a while. That is why a borderline result is usually repeated once you are well.
pages.biomarkerTsh.faqs[2].a: Yes. TSH often falls in early pregnancy, and many labs and clinicians use lower, trimester-specific ranges. If you are pregnant or planning to be, ask your clinician which range applies to you.
pages.biomarkerTsh.faqs[3].a: Fasting is usually not needed for TSH alone. Many clinicians prefer a morning test for consistency, and if you take thyroid medication you may be asked to take it after the blood draw.
pages.biomarkerTsh.faqs[3].q: Should I fast before a TSH test?
pages.biomarkerTsh.headline: TSH Test Explained: What a High or Low Thyroid Result Means
pages.biomarkerTsh.keywords: TSH test, TSH blood test, high TSH, low TSH, TSH normal range, thyroid blood test, what does high TSH mean, free T4, underactive thyroid test
pages.biomarkerTsh.lede: TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone, is usually the first blood test for checking how your thyroid is working. It moves in the opposite direction to what many people expect: a high TSH often means the thyroid is underactive, and a low TSH that it is overactive. This guide explains the ranges and what usually comes next.
pages.biomarkerTsh.rangesNote: mIU/L and µIU/mL are the same value. Ranges differ in pregnancy, in older adults and between labs. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[0].label: Usual adult range
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[0].value: About 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L (labs vary, often up to 4.5)
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[1].label: Mildly high
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[1].value: About 4.5 to 10 mIU/L, often rechecked before any treatment
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[2].label: Clearly high
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[2].value: Above 10 mIU/L, suggests an underactive thyroid
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[3].label: Low
pages.biomarkerTsh.ranges[3].value: Below about 0.4 mIU/L, may suggest an overactive thyroid
pages.biomarkerTsh.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[0].body: TSH is made by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. It tells the thyroid gland in your neck to make thyroid hormones, mainly T4 and some T3, which set the pace of your metabolism. When thyroid hormone levels drop, the pituitary releases more TSH to push the thyroid harder; when they rise, TSH falls.
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[0].title: What is TSH?
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[1].body: A high TSH usually means the thyroid is not making enough hormone, called hypothyroidism or an underactive thyroid. In many countries the most common cause is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition. Symptoms can include tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, constipation, dry skin and low mood, though many people with a mildly high TSH feel well.
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[1].title: What a high TSH usually means
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[2].body: A low TSH often means the thyroid is making too much hormone, called hyperthyroidism or an overactive thyroid, for example from Graves’ disease or thyroid nodules. It can also be low if you take more thyroid medication than you need. Symptoms can include a fast heartbeat, anxiety, weight loss, tremor, feeling hot and trouble sleeping.
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[2].title: What a low TSH usually means
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[3].body: If TSH is outside the range, the next test is usually free T4, and sometimes T3. A high TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism; a high TSH with a low free T4 is overt hypothyroidism. Thyroid antibodies, such as TPO antibodies, can show whether an autoimmune cause is likely.
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[3].title: Free T4, T3 and thyroid antibodies
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[4].body: TSH can shift with illness, recovery from illness, pregnancy, some medicines (including steroids, amiodarone and lithium) and the time of day; it tends to be higher in the early morning. High-dose biotin supplements can interfere with some lab methods, so mention them before the test. A single slightly abnormal result is often repeated in six to twelve weeks.
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[4].title: Things that can affect your TSH result
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[5].body: People who take levothyroxine are usually rechecked six to eight weeks after a dose change, then about once a year when stable. Taking the tablet the same way each day, on an empty stomach and apart from calcium, iron and coffee, keeps levels steadier. Any dose change is a decision for you and your clinician.
pages.biomarkerTsh.sections[5].title: If you take thyroid medication
pages.biomarkerTsh.seoDescription: What a TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) result means: typical ranges, why a high TSH points to an underactive thyroid and a low TSH to an overactive one, and what is tested next.

pages.biomarkerVitaminD.disclaimerBody: This guide is general information and does not replace personal medical advice. Talk to your clinician about your results and what they mean for you.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[0].a: Below 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) is generally considered deficient. Between 12 and 20 ng/mL (30 to 50 nmol/L) is low for some people. Many labs flag anything below 20 or 30 ng/mL, so ask your clinician which target applies to you.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[0].q: What vitamin D level is too low?
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[1].a: Low vitamin D can cause bone pain and muscle weakness, and some people with deficiency feel tired. Tiredness has many causes, though, and trials have not shown that vitamin D improves energy in people whose levels are already adequate.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[1].q: Can low vitamin D make you tired?
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[2].a: With a regular supplement, blood levels usually rise over several weeks and level off after about two to three months. Clinicians often recheck after about three months if the first result was low.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[2].q: How long does it take to raise vitamin D?
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[3].a: Many health bodies suggest a modest daily supplement, often 400 to 1,000 IU (10 to 25 micrograms), for groups at higher risk or during winter. Higher doses should be guided by a test and your clinician, because too much vitamin D can be harmful.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.faqs[3].q: Should I take vitamin D without a test?
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.headline: Vitamin D Test Explained: What Your 25-Hydroxyvitamin D Level Means
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.keywords: vitamin D test, vitamin D blood test, low vitamin D, vitamin D deficiency, vitamin D normal range, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, vitamin D levels ng/mL, nmol/L vitamin D, vitamin D insufficiency
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.lede: The usual vitamin D blood test measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the form that reflects how much vitamin D you get from sunlight, food and supplements. Low levels are common, especially in winter. Experts do not fully agree on the ideal level, so this guide explains the main ranges, who is most likely to run low, and how to raise it without overdoing it.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.rangesNote: To convert, multiply ng/mL by 2.5 to get nmol/L. Labs and guidelines use different cut-offs. Always use the reference range printed on your own report.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.ranges[0].label: Deficient
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.ranges[1].label: Low or insufficient for some people
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.ranges[2].label: Adequate for most people
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.ranges[2].value: 20 ng/mL or higher (50 nmol/L or higher); some labs aim for 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L)
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.ranges[3].label: Higher than needed
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.ranges[4].label: Risk of toxicity
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.secondaryCta: Meet ECHNA, your AI health assistant
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[0].body: Your skin makes vitamin D in sunlight, and you also get it from oily fish, egg yolks, fortified foods and supplements. The liver turns it into 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which stays in the blood for weeks and is the best measure of your overall vitamin D status. The active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, is a different test and is not used to check for deficiency.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[0].titl: What does the vitamin D test measure?
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[1].body: Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium and phosphate, which keep bones and muscles healthy. Long-term deficiency can lead to soft, weak bones (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults) and adds to the risk of osteoporosis. Low vitamin D has also been linked with many other conditions, but large trials have not shown that supplements prevent most of them in people who are not deficient.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[2].body: Low levels are more common in winter and at northern latitudes, in people who spend little time outdoors or cover most of their skin, in people with darker skin, in older adults, and in people with obesity. Conditions that affect fat absorption, such as coeliac disease, Crohn’s disease or weight-loss surgery, and some medicines, including certain anti-seizure drugs and steroids, can also lower vitamin D.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[2].titl: Who is most likely to run low
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[3].body: Some expert groups consider 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) enough for bone health in most people, while others have used 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) as a goal, especially for people at risk of bone disease. That is why the same result can be flagged as low by one lab and normal by another. Your clinician will look at your result with your bone health, diet and risk factors.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[4].body: Yes, but almost always from taking high-dose supplements for a long time, not from sunlight or food. Very high levels can raise blood calcium, causing nausea, thirst, frequent urination, confusion and, over time, kidney problems. Daily intake above 4,000 IU (100 micrograms) is generally not advised for adults unless a clinician recommends it.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[4].titl: Can vitamin D be too high?
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[5].body: Some time outdoors in daylight, oily fish, eggs and fortified foods help, but many people with low levels need a supplement, particularly in winter. Common daily doses for adults are 400 to 2,000 IU (10 to 50 micrograms); people who are deficient may be given a higher dose for a set time. It usually takes about two to three months for levels to settle, so a recheck is often done after that.
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.sections[5].titl: How vitamin D is raised safely
pages.biomarkerVitaminD.seoDescription: What a vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D) result means: deficient, adequate and high ranges in ng/mL and nmol/L, who runs low, and how vitamin D is raised safely.
